title: Conventions of Space and Time

jokes.text: But it will probably be London during the blitz.
jokes.setup: Troy and Jeff are excited about the Inspector Spacetime universe — they can go anywhere in time and space.
jokes.punchline: Abed deflates the fantasy by deadpanning that it will probably be London during the blitz — the worst possible destination.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Abed — he deconstructs the wish-fulfillment fantasy of the show with a single bleak historical footnote. The economy is excellent; the character integration is high because only Abed would phrase enthusiasm this way. Good opener.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And yet somehow we always end up in World War II London.

jokes.text: No. No. Abed's fragile. We have to ease him into it, okay? Do we want him to freak out and have to rescue him from some world where submarines are small enough to enter the bloodstream?
jokes.setup: Britta asks if they can just tell Abed they're sleeping together.
jokes.punchline: Troy's warning escalates into a hyper-specific absurdist scenario — Abed retreating into a world where miniature submarines can enter the bloodstream — referencing their established pattern of rescuing Abed from fantasy spirals.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: it's a callback to the show's mythology (Abed has broken from reality before), it's a surreal sci-fi riff, and it's perfect Troy — he cares deeply about Abed and the specificity of 'submarines small enough to enter the bloodstream' is delightfully unhinged. High character integration score because only Troy, terrified of losing his best friend dynamic, would generate this exact image.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We need to ease Abed into this. If we just tell him we're dating, he might have a complete breakdown. I'm talking full Fantastic Voyage scenario—he'll shrink down to microscopic size and get injected into someone's bloodstream.

jokes.text: I totally wanna do that.
jokes.setup: Troy has described a worst-case scenario (Abed lost in a miniature submarine world) as a warning against telling Abed about their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Britta's immediate, sincere enthusiasm for the scenario undercuts Troy's alarm entirely.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum impact. Britta's oblivious enthusiasm perfectly characterizes her — she missed the point entirely and found the sci-fi scenario appealing. Great economy and solid character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yes! Finally! I've been waiting for this my whole life!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What do you need me to do? Do I get a cape? Can I have a cape?

jokes.text: Troy, it's a week away, and we need to revise our whole strategy... I've printed out several maps of the convention center and color-coded the best potential routes. I have longer strides, but your superior physical fitness will allow you to compensate with greater speed.
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy are preparing for InSpecTiCon.
jokes.punchline: Abed has approached a fan convention with the tactical precision of a military operation, complete with color-coded maps and a biomechanical analysis of their complementary running capabilities.
jokes.explanation: Pure Abed — the hyper-literal tactical analysis of a recreational convention is exactly his brand of comedy. The physical breakdown of their respective advantages is the high point. Character integration is as strong as it gets.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Hey Abed, what's up?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: 14 hours and 37 minutes since I last saw you. You got a haircut.

jokes.text: We need to save time by changing into our costumes in the car. [Cut to: curling iron being handed between them.]
jokes.setup: Abed announces they need to change in the car for efficiency.
jokes.punchline: The implied visual: Troy is using a curling iron as part of his costume prep, suggesting an elaborate and very uncasual process happening in a moving vehicle. The deadpan handoff sells it.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely visual — the contrast between Abed's military efficiency framing and the implied reality (curling iron in a car) is a sharp sight gag. The economy of the transcript's 'Curling iron. Thanks.' is perfect deadpan. Rewatch bonus because viewers will clock what it implies.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've known about you two for three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? How?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're not as subtle as you think. Also, I have access to the security camera footage.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: There are security cameras in our dorm?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: There are security cameras everywhere. I'm just the only one who watches them.

jokes.text: I haven't seen you in over 12 hours. Ha, ha. Yeah. I know you two are having sex. I've known for weeks. What? Why didn't you say something? I love doughnuts.
jokes.setup: Britta gives a flimsy cover story for being at the apartment early. Abed calmly reveals he already knows about the relationship. Troy and Britta are shocked and ask why he didn't say anything.
jokes.punchline: "I love doughnuts" — a complete non-sequitur that is somehow a perfect Abed answer. It signals both that he's comfortable with the situation and that he operates on a different conversational wavelength than everyone else.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup carefully builds expectation — Abed knows, there must be a reason he stayed quiet — and then completely subverts the anticipated emotional explanation with a non sequitur about doughnuts. But it's not random: it perfectly captures Abed's social wiring. He had his own reasons, they're opaque to others, and he's moved on. The quotability is extremely high — this is the kind of line fans repeat. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know about you two.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Anyway, has anyone seen those Boston cream doughnuts? They had them in the cafeteria this morning.

jokes.text: You don't need sunglasses to go to an Inspector Spacetime convention. For an Inspector Spacetime convention, I'd need a bag to put over my head.
jokes.setup: Jeff has his sunglasses. Someone questions why he needs them for the convention.
jokes.punchline: Jeff corrects the expectation: sunglasses aren't sufficient. He'd need to hide his entire face — positioning the convention as deeply embarrassing to be associated with.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff — the escalation from 'sunglasses' to 'bag over my head' is a well-constructed one-two. It's very Jeff-specific: his obsession with coolness and disdain for nerd culture. The structure is clean. Not groundbreaking but well-executed character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You don't need sunglasses, Jeff. We're indoors.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not worried about the sun, Annie. I'm worried about someone seeing me here.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: At a sci-fi convention?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: At a place where grown men are dressed as Klingons. Yes.

jokes.text: And what's this about a road trip? Look, Pierce, no one was trying to leave you out. We just assumed you wouldn't be interested. Which is why we left you out.
jokes.setup: Jeff tries to soften Pierce's feelings by saying they weren't trying to leave him out — they just assumed he wouldn't be interested.
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately undercuts his own reassurance: "Which is why we left you out." He can't help but be brutally honest, destroying the diplomatic cover he just laid.
jokes.explanation: Sharp structural joke — the setup and punchline are contained within consecutive sentences. Jeff says the diplomatic thing and then immediately eviscerates it. Very Jeff: he can't sustain social grace for more than four words. The structure (correction immediately following the comfort) is tight and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I want to go on your trip. What do you call yourselves again?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We're just a study group.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh, so I'll be joining Studying Group on their adventure!

jokes.text: Why can't I go to a Captain Warptime convention?
jokes.setup: The group has been discussing the Inspector Spacetime convention.
jokes.punchline: Pierce has not absorbed a single word — he has the wrong name entirely ('Captain Warptime' vs 'Inspector Spacetime'), revealing total disengagement.
jokes.explanation: A reliable Pierce joke — he's fundamentally disconnected from what everyone else is talking about. The wrong name is a good specific detail. Not exceptional but well-deployed for the character.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I belong here! Back in Ancient Greece, they had space conventions too, you know. Yeah, that's right - the Spartans were launching shuttles while you people were still figuring out the wheel!

jokes.text: In ancient Greece, it was considered an honor to invite a person my age to a space convention?
jokes.setup: Pierce is protesting being left out, trying to make his case for inclusion.
jokes.punchline: Pierce invokes 'ancient Greece' as an authority for a completely fabricated cultural norm — and frames it as a question, undermining his own argument. The 'ancient Greece' crutch is his go-to for invented wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Pierce's 'ancient Greece' gambit is a running character trait — he invents historical precedent to legitimize his positions. The question mark at the end is a nice touch, suggesting even Pierce isn't sure he's right. Solid character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The Inspector has had several female companions throughout the years.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, and we don't hate them because they're women. We hate them because they're poorly written.

jokes.text: We didn't invite Shirley either. Well, that's better then.
jokes.setup: Pierce is upset about being excluded from the trip.
jokes.punchline: The moment Jeff reveals Shirley was also excluded, Pierce's wounded dignity instantly evaporates — being excluded alongside someone else is enough for him.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical two-beat exchange. Pierce's objection isn't about fairness — it's about relative status. Learning Shirley was also excluded satisfies his competitive ego entirely. The 'Well, that's better then' is a sharp character revelation delivered with ideal economy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Al Capone? More like Al Ca-GONE!

jokes.text: It's beautiful. [Troy and Abed arrive at the convention, visibly moved.]
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed arrive at InSpecTiCon.
jokes.punchline: Their genuine, reverent awe at a nerd convention — described with the emotional register of witnessing a natural wonder — is the joke. The sincerity is the comedy.
jokes.explanation: A simple but effective moment — the gap between the grandeur of their reaction and the reality of a sci-fi convention is the joke. Elevated by their genuine emotional investment, which is core to Troy and Abed's charm.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Why is everyone staring at you?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because I'm the most attractive person here.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We're at a comic book convention.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: She can wait in the car.
jokes.setup: Troy asks if it's okay that Britta is there.
jokes.punchline: Abed's casual suggestion that Britta wait in the car — not out of malice but matter-of-fact logistical thinking — is perfectly Abed.
jokes.explanation: Four words, completely in character. Abed has no social malice but also no social filter. The economy is near perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why is everyone staring at me?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff, you look exactly like The Dark Elf from Game of Thrones.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? No, I don't.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You really do. It's uncanny.

jokes.text: Was there a female inspector? Everyone hates her. Not because they're sexist. She sucks.
jokes.setup: Britta notices an Inspector Spacetime character and asks if there was a female inspector.
jokes.punchline: Abed's immediate, clinical dismissal — preemptively ruling out sexism as a motive before affirming she just 'sucks' — is a sharp meta-joke about fandom's complicated relationship with female characters in genre shows (a clear Doctor Who reference).
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. It's a layered meta-commentary on the Doctor Who fandom's historically contentious relationship with female versions of beloved characters, delivered through Abed's voice in a way that's funny AND somewhat self-aware. The structure — anticipating and preemptively dismissing the sexism charge — is clever and economical. The bluntness of 'She sucks' after the defense is the punchline. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: This is my first adult vacation. You know how I know I'm an adult? I'm staying at a hotel with a continental breakfast.

jokes.text: Britta. Annie. You're on your own, Al Capone.
jokes.setup: Britta and Annie arrive at the convention together and apparently pair off, leaving someone behind.
jokes.punchline: Calling the abandoned party 'Al Capone' — a gangster nickname that makes no contextual sense — lands as an absurd, throwaway non sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing but undercooked. The 'Al Capone' non sequitur doesn't land with enough conviction to be truly absurdist, and the character integration is weak — it's not specifically Britta or Annie. Gets a mild chuckle but doesn't earn its place.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I will! And... and you'll enjoy being... tall and stupid!

jokes.text: Abed was just showing that he's accepting of our relationship. No, really. What was it?
jokes.setup: Abed's 'I love doughnuts' non-sequitur has just confused everyone. Britta offers a generous psychological interpretation.
jokes.punchline: Troy dismisses her framing entirely and asks for the actual explanation — a moment of Troy knowing Abed well enough to know something stranger was happening.
jokes.explanation: A beat that extends the doughnut joke. Britta psychologizes, Troy cuts through it. Good character contrast — Britta over-interprets, Troy under-interprets. Functions well as a callback extension.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: My friend Toby almost couldn't make it from Nigeria.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Apparently he's a prince and needs help transferring money out of the country.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I told him I'd wire him my entire savings account, but then I realized—that's probably not how it works.

jokes.text: Hey, Annie, sad news. They closed the ski slopes. A dozen scouts got buried in an avalanche. So sad. I say we cut our losses and head home.
jokes.setup: Jeff desperately wants to leave the convention.
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers the news of a deadly avalanche burying scouts with performative sadness, then immediately pivots to 'I say we cut our losses and head home' — his self-interest is so naked that the tragedy is just a pretext.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's moral flexibility is well-deployed here — the scouts are dead, that's sad, moving on. The pivot is clean and character-specific. 'So sad' as a throwaway line before the ask is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: Thanks for the money, Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: You know, it's funny. Everyone ignores those Nigerian prince emails, but when a real Nigerian prince asks for money, suddenly I'm the weird one.

jokes.text: I'd have more fun hanging out with the parents that are circling the block.
jokes.setup: Annie suggests they hang out at the convention since they're already there.
jokes.punchline: Jeff suggests the convention parking lot, where parents are waiting to pick up their children, would be more fun than the convention itself — implying the attendees are childlike.
jokes.explanation: A solid Jeff line that plays on the nerd convention stereotype without being mean-spirited. The specificity of 'circling the block' elevates it above a generic put-down.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: His wife is always complaining about something. She's never happy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, she's like the Blorgons from Inspector Spacetime — always invading and ruining everything.

jokes.text: Why are people staring at you? They've never seen a man who's had sex before?
jokes.setup: People at the convention are staring at Jeff. He looks notably out of place.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's explanation — that convention attendees are virginal and stunned by the sight of a sexually active man — is both egotistical and a convention-crowd stereotype delivered with his signature arrogance.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's vanity and his condescension toward convention culture combine here effectively. The phrasing is sharp. Leans slightly on the nerd-stereotype crutch but Jeff's delivery context elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, Minerva? That's a girl's name, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I just called the Inspector a girl. She's gonna think I was being sexist.

jokes.text: You bear resemblance to Inspector Spacetime's super villain Thoraxis.
jokes.setup: People are staring at Jeff at the convention.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Jeff resembles the show's villain — and the implicit joke that this is not flattering but that the fans find it exciting — recontextualizes why he's being stared at.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the 'why are people staring' setup. Also seeds the later hotel bar subplot. Rewatch bonus because it sets up Thoraxis gag payoffs later.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone needs to blend in. Act natural. We're just here to watch... uh... The Office?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, that's not even a real show.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I know that! I was testing you!

jokes.text: Okay. Now we're definitely leaving.
jokes.setup: Jeff is told he looks like a supervillain at the sci-fi convention.
jokes.punchline: Rather than finding this funny or flattering, Jeff treats it as the final indignity that justifies departure — the reaction beat is funnier than any explicit joke.
jokes.explanation: Economical character beat. Jeff's wounded dignity at being compared to a villain is funny given his normal confidence. The escalating indignities Jeff suffers at the convention are building nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, what? No, no, we're huge fans! I've seen every episode! Well, not every episode, but like... a lot of episodes. Which episodes have you seen? Do you have a favorite character? Mine changes weekly. Is that normal? Do real fans have a favorite character or do they love everyone equally? Oh God, I'm sweating. Why am I sweating? Do I look nervous? I'm not nervous!

jokes.text: I've never been on an adult vacation. This is the first time I've stayed in a hotel without a number in its name.
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to convince Jeff to stay at the convention hotel.
jokes.punchline: Annie's revelation that this is her first hotel experience without a number in the name (Holiday Inn 8, Super 8, Motel 6, etc.) is a sharp class-marker joke that tells us everything about her background and financial situation.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. It's a quietly devastating character detail — Annie's financial background, her sheltered life, her genuine excitement about something Jeff takes for granted. The specificity of 'without a number in its name' is what elevates it from a generic 'Annie is poor' joke to something precise and observational. Highly quotable and character-defining. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yes, hello, I'd like to order dinner for two. No, no carbs please, we're watching our figure. Oh, and a bottle of your finest wine. Actually, make it two bottles.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What? I'm being health-conscious and romantic!

jokes.text: "Jeff won." / "I know."
jokes.setup: Jeff abandons the group to go to his room, refusing to engage with the convention.
jokes.punchline: Annie flatly acknowledges Jeff's power move worked. Britta confirms. The resigned, matter-of-fact acceptance of Jeff's social dominance is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Four words, great rhythm. Acknowledging Jeff's social manipulation as a 'win' treats the interaction like a competitive game, which is both meta and character-consistent. Quick but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The kind that makes you forget you're in a hotel room with a girl who ironed her jeans.

jokes.text: Jeff won. I know.
jokes.setup: Jeff announces he'll be in his room and storms off, leaving the convention to the group.
jokes.punchline: Britta and Troy quietly acknowledge Jeff's victory in getting what he wanted — the hotel room — while the group stays at the convention. The resigned acknowledgment is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-timed beat. The collective recognition that Jeff's tantrum was actually strategically successful is a sharp group-dynamic joke. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: We have every right to be here at this convention. We're not sexist, we're not racist, we're not ageist, we're not heightist—we're just very specific about our preferences.

jokes.text: You've been busy lately having sex.
jokes.setup: Troy is surprised Abed never mentioned Toby, his new friend.
jokes.punchline: Abed's matter-of-fact explanation for why he hadn't mentioned Toby — Troy was preoccupied with sex — is delivered with zero judgment or irony, which is exactly what makes it funny.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed deadpan — he states the unsexy truth (his friend has been having sex, hence unavailable) with clinical neutrality. The character integration is high because the joke only works with Abed's specific affect.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You're worried they're gonna break up? Troy, they're not in a relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know, but—

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, see, that's your problem. You're applying relationship logic to a friendship. It doesn't work that way. When two people are just friends, they can drift apart without it being a tragedy. It's actually healthy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But what if they stop talking completely?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Then they'll reconnect later, or they won't. Either way, you don't get to have feelings about it because you're not involved. You're like a relationship therapist trying to save a marriage that doesn't exist.

jokes.text: He works in Nigeria in banking. He almost couldn't come. His money was tied up. I sent him £700 and a plane ticket. He should be here.
jokes.setup: Abed introduces Toby, his online friend he's excited to meet.
jokes.punchline: The cascade of details — Nigeria, banking, money tied up, Abed sent him £700 and a plane ticket — is a textbook Nigerian prince email scam description delivered by Abed with complete sincerity. The audience realizes before Abed does that he's been scammed.
jokes.explanation: A slow-burn setup that lands beautifully. Abed's sincerity makes it funnier — he's describing a classic internet scam with complete trust. The beat of 'Oh, Abed' from someone in the group (the audience surrogate) acknowledges the horror without over-explaining. The rewatch bonus is high because on rewatch you catch each detail as a scam tell. Very well-constructed joke.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So if I love someone, I just... let them go? What if they get hit by a bus? What if they join a cult? What if they become a bus that joins a cult?

jokes.text: Where's your constable? My best friend Andrew. His wife wouldn't let him go at the last minute. She's such a Minerva. Yeah, yeah. Minerva, what a bitch.
jokes.setup: Toby asks about Troy's 'constable' (best friend), mirroring the Inspector/Constable dynamic from the show. Toby explains his friend Andrew couldn't come because of his wife.
jokes.punchline: Troy enthusiastically agrees that Andrew's wife is a 'Minerva' (the show's controlling female villain) — but Troy has no idea who Minerva is and is clearly just performing solidarity. His enthusiasm ('Yeah, yeah. Minerva, what a bitch.') reveals he's faking knowledge to bond with Toby.
jokes.explanation: A good joke about the social performance of fandom — Troy is enthusiastically agreeing with references he doesn't understand to fit in. 'What a bitch' as a cap to vocabulary he doesn't know is a fun character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I'll tell you what. The production values are top-notch, the writing is extraordinarily clever, and the lead actor has real gravitas. But here's the thing - and I say this with all due respect - I haven't the faintest idea what's going on. Not a clue. It's like watching Shakespeare performed by aliens who learned English phonetically.

jokes.text: Was that the female inspector? Not in front of Toby.
jokes.setup: Britta asks if Minerva was the female inspector.
jokes.punchline: Abed's urgent 'Not in front of Toby' — as if the mere mention of the female inspector could cause offense — is an escalation of the earlier female inspector joke, suggesting this is a hot-button fandom topic.
jokes.explanation: A good callback that extends the female inspector running gag. Abed's protectiveness about the topic in front of a guest is a funny social beat — the fandom lore as a minefield to navigate.

dialogue.speaker: Fan 1
dialogue.line: Do the thing! Do the Thoraxis thing!

dialogue.speaker: Fan 2
dialogue.line: Yeah! Say the line!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Fan 1
dialogue.line: Come on, Thoraxis! 'Bite my shiny metal...!'

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not Thoraxis, I'm just a guy at a convention.

dialogue.speaker: Multiple Fans
dialogue.line: DO IT! DO IT! DO IT!

jokes.text: Which inspector would win in a fight in space? / Which inspector would win in a fight in time?
jokes.setup: Toby reveals he has tickets to sold-out panels.
jokes.punchline: The panel topics are revealed as two separate events that differ only by replacing 'space' with 'time' — the panels are both extremely specific and also completely redundant to each other.
jokes.explanation: A good parody of fan convention panel culture — the panels are both hyper-specific and self-replicating in the way real convention panels often are. The parallel structure (space/time) is a neat comedic construction.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Hey Toby, it's me, Troy! Troy Barnes!

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: Sorry, do I know you?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We met in Spanish class? I'm on the football team? I do impressions?

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: Doesn't ring a bell.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I sang 'Somewhere Over the Rainbow' in the study room! You were there!

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: Nope.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay, remember when I dressed up as a dinosaur? Or when I got shot with a paintball? Or when I—

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: I really don't know who you are.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But... but I'm Troy! I'm in your life! I exist! I'm REAL!

jokes.text: Are you sure Troy and Abed want us here? They do. They just don't know it yet.
jokes.setup: Pierce and Shirley have crashed the convention despite not being invited.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's confident assertion that Troy and Abed want them there despite being unaware of it is simultaneously delusional and charmingly optimistic. The logic is perfectly inverted.
jokes.explanation: A solid Shirley beat — her gentle confidence in the face of obvious social unwantedness is a good character note. Not a standout but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: I'm thinking we do a morning show pairing. You and Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? No. Abed and I have nothing in common.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're completely different people.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We both like TV and film.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay, well, besides that obvious thing, we have nothing in common.

jokes.text: Remember, we're a couple of Captain Warphead fans. Nobody will even notice we're here.
jokes.setup: Pierce and Shirley are disguising themselves as fans to blend in.
jokes.punchline: Shirley uses yet another wrong name for the show ('Captain Warphead') — a callback to Pierce's 'Captain Warptime' — while also claiming they won't be noticed, despite visibly sticking out.
jokes.explanation: A callback to Pierce's wrong name but now Shirley has her own wrong version. The irony of 'nobody will notice us' is predictable but the specific wrong name adds a little texture.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: London is amazing. It's got Big Ben, it's got the Crown Jewels, it's got this legend...

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What legend?

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: The Underground.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's just a subway system.

jokes.text: Convention security escorts Pierce and Shirley away to 'help with something' — they are immediately recruited the moment they arrive.
jokes.setup: Pierce confidently claims they won't be noticed. Convention security immediately approaches.
jokes.punchline: Instead of being thrown out for being obvious impostors, they're recruited — the convention apparently needs two clearly out-of-place non-fans for a 'focus group.'
jokes.explanation: Setup for the focus-group subplot. Adequate plot machinery but not especially funny on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff, why do you need a hair dryer? Your hair is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Thank you, Annie. A lawyer's appearance is everything.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So you're saying your hair is part of your legal strategy?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Objection: assumes facts not in evidence. But yes.

jokes.text: Excuse me. Oh, yes? Will you come with us? Where? Why? When? Okay.
jokes.setup: Pierce and Shirley claim they'll blend in and nobody will notice them.
jokes.punchline: They are immediately approached and taken away by convention staff — the instant, complete failure of their blending-in plan. The 'Where? Why? When? Okay.' suggests they give in without any resistance.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the 'nobody will notice' setup delivered within seconds. The rapid capitulation ('Okay.') is a funny beat — they don't even try to maintain their cover. Sets up the focus group subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I think the show should stay true to what makes it special. It's about these characters and their genuine connections.

dialogue.speaker: Focus Group Moderator
dialogue.line: That's great, but what if we just made everything more explosive? Like, literally. Explosions in every scene.

jokes.text: Room service. Yes, I'd like to order some food. And how many people will be dining today, Mrs. Winger?
jokes.setup: Annie is in Jeff's hotel room, begins calling room service.
jokes.punchline: The hotel staff addresses her as 'Mrs. Winger' — revealing that Annie has already registered herself as Jeff's wife, before we even see the full extent of her fantasy.
jokes.explanation: Good reveal structure — we don't know yet what Annie has done, but 'Mrs. Winger' lands as an immediate, specific surprise. Sets up an entire subplot efficiently. The rewatch bonus is for noticing Annie's not-quite-surprised reaction to being called Mrs. Winger.

dialogue.speaker: Convention Attendee
dialogue.line: Wait, Thoraxis is married? To a real person?

dialogue.speaker: Convention Attendee
dialogue.line: That means his wife is married to a villain who destroys entire civilizations.

dialogue.speaker: Convention Attendee
dialogue.line: She probably can't even keep a houseplant alive around him.

jokes.text: Two. Yeah, I'd like a turkey burger and a second turkey burger, but with no bun. My husband doesn't do carbs. But he would like a scotch. And what kind of scotch would your husband prefer? The good kind.
jokes.setup: Annie is ordering room service as 'Mrs. Winger,' playing out a marriage fantasy.
jokes.punchline: Annie knows Jeff's specific dietary preferences (no carbs) and his scotch habit — but when asked what kind of scotch, she can only say 'the good kind,' revealing she's been fantasizing about him from the outside, not from actual intimacy.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke with layered character revelation. Annie knows Jeff's surface preferences (no carbs, scotch) but blanks on specifics ('the good kind') — which precisely defines the nature of her fantasy. It's aspirational but incomplete. The specificity of 'no bun' vs. the vagueness of 'the good kind' is a lovely contrast. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I'd rather be back in one of those classic anxiety dreams where I show up to class naked and unprepared. At least then I'd wake up and realize none of it was real. This? This is real, and I'm still not prepared.

jokes.text: Yes, Mrs. Winger? [Annie poses with cigarette holder or similar glamour prop at the window, playing the fantasy to the hilt.]
jokes.setup: Annie is fully inhabiting her 'Mrs. Winger' fantasy in the hotel room.
jokes.punchline: The visual of Annie acting out a full period-drama wife fantasy — presumably posed glamorously — when she's actually a college student in a sci-fi convention hotel is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A visual beat inferred from context. The comedy is in Annie's total commitment to the fantasy. The humor is primarily visual and relies on the performance, which we can only infer.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I got you something to cheer you up! It's a limited edition collectible action figure.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Britta, this is a My Little Pony doll.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yeah, and? It's limited edition. The guy at the store said so.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You bought this at a toy store, didn't you?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, I bought it at a very sophisticated collectibles shop. It was right next to the Sanrio store.

jokes.text: Call me Nige.
jokes.setup: Someone addresses the actor who played Thoraxis (the supervillain Jeff resembles) by his full name.
jokes.punchline: 'Call me Nige' — a diminutive of Nigel that's endearingly normal for someone who played a space supervillain — is a funny deflation of expected celebrity pomposity.
jokes.explanation: Two words, works as a quick character establishment. The gap between the gravity of playing a supervillain and 'Call me Nige' is a compact joke. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, you said your name was Steve last week.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: No I didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yes you did. You told me about when you were in the Peace Corps in Peru.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: That was... that was a different story.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, Toby—or should I say Steve—you literally introduced yourself as Steve.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: I would never—

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You're doing it right now. You're lying right now.

jokes.text: No. Troy, I have seen that look. Girls have given me that look. You are not being crazy. That dude is trying to steal your boyfriend.
jokes.setup: Troy is visibly unsettled watching Abed bond with Toby.
jokes.punchline: Britta identifies exactly what's happening — Toby is trying to 'steal' Abed — framing it in romantic jealousy terms ('steal your boyfriend'), which is both accurate and funny given Troy and Abed's bromance.
jokes.explanation: Good joke that plays on Troy and Abed's relationship being coded as a bromance. Britta applying the 'steal your boyfriend' framework is both accurate and funny — the show has always treated Troy and Abed's friendship as a kind of love story. Britta's self-referential 'girls have given me that look' adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: I'm superior to neurotypicals. My brain is simply more advanced.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, Inspector Spacetime teaches us that true advancement isn't about being superior—it's about connection. The Inspector's greatest strength was his friendships across dimensions and species.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Your neurotype doesn't make you better or worse. It just makes you different. And difference is what makes a group stronger, not weaker.

jokes.text: I mean, what if Abed wants to replace me? It makes me so angry and sad all at the same time.
jokes.setup: Troy is opening up about his fear of Toby replacing him.
jokes.punchline: Troy's raw, unguarded emotional articulation ('angry and sad all at the same time') is nakedly sincere in a way that's both endearing and funny — played against Britta as the relationship advice surrogate.
jokes.explanation: Troy's emotional transparency is always a source of comedy — his sincere expression of 'angry and sad' in this context treats his friendship with Abed with the gravity of a romantic relationship. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: Look, Abed, I know this is a difficult situation, but I brought you a cappuccino from that place you like.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You kidnapped me.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: I know, but I also got you a bagel. A fresh one. Still warm.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm calling the police.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: Wait—what if I also throw in a movie night? We could watch whatever you want.

jokes.text: Because for some reason, men find these feelings to be psycho. And if you freak out, it's only gonna push Abed away.
jokes.setup: Britta is giving Troy relationship advice about managing jealousy over Toby.
jokes.punchline: Britta is accurately diagnosing a romantic relationship dynamic — applied to a friendship — while completely unaware that she's perfectly describing how she handles her own relationships. The irony is that Britta gives competent advice she can't follow herself.
jokes.explanation: Situationally ironic — Britta dispenses solid relationship advice while being famously terrible at relationships herself. The character note is consistent and functional.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Have you ever been in a fight?

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: No! Why would I be in a fight?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I don't know, man. Just asking.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: Well, I haven't. Fights are barbaric.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but what if someone just... punched you?

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'punched' me? Like with their fist?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Toby
dialogue.line: That's a closed hand moving at high velocity. That would hurt!

jokes.text: Like I always say, if you love someone, set them free. And if they don't come back to you, they were never yours to begin with. That makes no sense. What if they get hit or fall down a well?
jokes.setup: Britta delivers the classic 'set them free' relationship advice platitude.
jokes.punchline: Troy punctures it with a completely literal, logistics-based counterargument: what if the person can't come back due to physical circumstance? His earnest, practical objection to the metaphor is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Troy takes the metaphor completely literally and his objection — 'what if they get hit or fall down a well?' — is both absurd and logically coherent from his perspective. The structure is clean (platitude → literal puncture), the character integration is perfect (Troy's earnest literalism), and the punchline is quotable. The 'fall down a well' specifically is a great absurdist image that elevates it above generic 'Troy is dumb' jokes. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Thanks for getting me out of the box, Troy. Though honestly, at this point, I've been in so many boxes I'm starting to think of them as my second home.

jokes.text: Remind me to not put you down as my emergency contact.
jokes.setup: Troy has just questioned the 'set them free' metaphor by asking about being hit or falling down a well.
jokes.punchline: Britta's response — ruling out Troy as an emergency contact — is a sharp, economical comeback that acknowledges his impracticality in a funny way.
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean callback punchline. 'Emergency contact' is an immediate, logical extension of the well/hit imagery. Well-timed and highly quotable as a standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, you fantasize about marrying me? That's... actually kind of flattering.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: But here's what I'm concerned about — if we did get married, would I start losing my hair? Because I've seen what happens to married men. The stress, the responsibility...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: My hair is basically my best feature. I can't risk that.

jokes.text: I was confused. And what confused you? The time travel mostly. Also the space travel. Anything else? How many clipboards you got?
jokes.setup: Pierce is in a focus group for the American Inspector Spacetime. Staff asks what confused him.
jokes.punchline: Pierce was confused by... all of Inspector Spacetime. When asked for more specifics, he turns the question back with 'How many clipboards you got?' — implying his list of confusions is endless and challenging the researcher's capacity to record them.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed bit. The escalation of Pierce's confusion (time travel... space travel...) and the pivot to 'how many clipboards you got?' is a funny structure — he transforms from focus group subject to someone indicting the entire focus group process. Good character integration: Pierce's total incomprehension made useful.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I've had fantasies about marrying different people. First it was Jeff, then Troy, then Abed, then Pierce, then Shirley, then the Dean, then Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But mostly just Abed.

jokes.text: Hey, do you mind if I practice my American accent? I have an audition.
jokes.setup: Nigel (Thoraxis) is chatting with Annie.
jokes.punchline: The actor who played a sci-fi villain wants to practice his American accent for an audition — the mundane reality of a character actor's career punctures the glamour of the fan convention world around him.
jokes.explanation: A light, functional joke about the gap between fan reverence and an actor's grinding career. It humanizes Nigel in a funny way. Not exceptional but solid character establishment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I would never cheat on you.

jokes.text: Bow before Thoraxis. This is my ringtone. Bow before Thoraxis.
jokes.setup: Nigel is mid-conversation having a sincere discussion about Inspector Spacetime.
jokes.punchline: His phone rings — and his ringtone is his own catchphrase from the show. The self-important villain catchphrase as a personal ringtone deflates any gravitas and is weirdly endearing.
jokes.explanation: A good situational joke — the actor whose villain catchphrase is 'Bow before Thoraxis' has set it as his own ringtone. It's self-aware vanity and also slightly pathetic in a funny way. The comedy is in the casual normality of his explanation: 'This is my ringtone.' Also sets up the later 'Say your catchphrase' callback.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Can I get an appletini?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: An appletini? Really? I'm not ordering that.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because I have to say the word 'appletini' out loud to a bartender.

jokes.text: This is so nice, just three friends, friending around all unthreatened-like.
jokes.setup: Troy has found Abed and Toby and is trying to play it cool.
jokes.punchline: 'Friending around all unthreatened-like' — Troy's invented phrase and the modifier 'unthreatened-like' completely gives away that he is very threatened. The word 'friending' is an awkward neologism that signals his discomfort.
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier Troy lines in the episode. The invented word 'friending' and the qualifier 'unthreatened-like' are perfect — the phrasing itself proves the opposite of what he's claiming. High character integration and high quotability. Very Troy in its earnest desperation.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Fine. Okay. Here it goes.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Cool. Cool cool cool.

jokes.text: Sorry. This is slightly embarrassing. I seem to have forgotten your name. It's Troy! You know it's Troy! Okay, it's the first part of Troy and Abed. Toby and Abed in the morning? That's ridiculous. I'm not psycho!
jokes.setup: Toby (possibly intentionally) claims he's forgotten Troy's name.
jokes.punchline: Troy's escalating fury — from 'It's Troy!' to 'You know it's Troy!' to the devastating realization that his name + Abed could become 'Toby and Abed' — culminating in the unprompted 'I'm not psycho!' is a perfect cringe escalation. The 'Troy and Abed in the Morning' callback makes it land harder.
jokes.explanation: A standout moment. The escalation is perfectly constructed — Troy holds it together until the specific threat of 'Troy and Abed in the Morning' becoming 'Toby and Abed in the Morning' breaks him. 'That's ridiculous' about his own name replacement, followed by 'I'm not psycho!' with no prompt, is a classic Community cringe beat. The audience has the full context of what 'Troy and Abed in the Morning' means, making the callback land hard. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Thoraxis!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I don't know what that is, and I'm not going to ask.

jokes.text: I've got your hair dryer, Mrs. Winger. Thank you, Randy, but it's not for me. It's for my husband. He needs the diffuser for his hair. It sounds shallow, but he's a lawyer.
jokes.setup: Annie is in full 'Mrs. Winger' mode in the hotel.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's vanity is so well-known to Annie that she's pre-ordered a hair diffuser for him in her fantasy — and her explanation ('he's a lawyer') perfectly captures how Jeff uses his profession as social armor for his appearance obsession.
jokes.explanation: Annie's intimate knowledge of Jeff's vanity habits (he needs the diffuser) paired with 'it sounds shallow, but he's a lawyer' is sharp — it both mocks Jeff and shows the depth of Annie's fantasy. The 'he's a lawyer' justification is very Jeff-ian.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Inspector Spacetime here. I've just realized I traveled back in time and married my own grandmother, which means I'm my own grandfather. And also... my own father. And mother. And I may have... inadvertently become my own son.

jokes.text: Actually, having dual careers has put a lot of stress on our marriage. Hence the separate rooms. But I think this trip is really gonna change all that. My husband will finally see me not as a world-famous police detective, but as a woman.
jokes.setup: Annie is elaborating on her 'Mrs. Winger' fantasy to the hotel staff.
jokes.punchline: The fantasy has escalated — Annie is now a 'world-famous police detective' in an increasingly baroque domestic drama. The specificity of 'world-famous police detective' as her fantasy profession is both absurd and revealing of how Annie's daydreams go full soap opera.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Annie's fantasy is well-deployed — she's gone from ordering room service to inventing a whole soap opera backstory. 'World-famous police detective' as her choice of alter ego is a funny specific detail that tells us about Annie's self-image aspirations. Rewatch bonus for catching how the fantasy keeps inflating.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is the dumbest thing I've ever seen.

jokes.text: Your husband's a lucky man. That he is.
jokes.setup: Annie has been spinning an elaborate fantasy about her fictional marriage to Jeff.
jokes.punchline: The hotel employee sincerely compliments the fictional Jeff, and Annie agrees with equal sincerity — the irony of Annie validating a compliment about a husband who doesn't exist and doesn't know any of this is happening.
jokes.explanation: A quiet, effective beat capping the fantasy sequence. 'That he is' — Annie fully endorsing the imaginary husband — is the right comedic punctuation. Economy is good.

jokes.text: Mm. Tastes of bog.
jokes.setup: Toby is at the focus group, apparently drinking something American.
jokes.punchline: 'Tastes of bog' — a brilliantly specific British complaint that tells us something is bad while being completely opaque to American ears.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words that are entirely character-specific. 'Tastes of bog' is delightfully specific British invective and immediately funny for its bluntness and specificity. Good character integration for Toby.

jokes.text: You see? It's funny because it's clear.
jokes.setup: Shirley is in the focus group, apparently hearing a joke from the American Inspector Spacetime pilot.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's critique — 'it's funny because it's clear' — is a devastating meta-commentary on lowest-common-denominator American TV comedy. She thinks clarity (i.e., broad, obvious jokes) is the virtue. The audience understands this is damning.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest meta-jokes in the episode. Shirley is inadvertently describing and endorsing lowest-common-denominator comedy — 'it's funny because it's clear' is an absolutely precise skewering of broad network TV humor. It's also a self-aware moment for Community itself, which prides itself on being the opposite. The economy is excellent and the meta-layer earns its score.

jokes.text: I think what they like about the show is that it's smart, complicated, doesn't talk down to its audience. So if you'd like to make a really good American version, you should stay true to that.
jokes.setup: Jeff, who doesn't watch Inspector Spacetime and is contemptuous of nerd culture, has been pulled into the focus group.
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers the most articulate, accurate defense of Inspector Spacetime — by proxy, defending Community itself — despite having no genuine investment in the show. The irony of the disengaged character making the most earnest appeal is sharp.
jokes.explanation: A meta-moment where Jeff becomes the show's mouthpiece. The irony is functional — the least interested character gives the most accurate diagnosis. It's also Community commenting on its own ambitions through Jeff. Rewatch bonus for the meta-layer.

jokes.text: Hey, instead of this constable, what about a blonde with long legs and a tennis racket?
jokes.setup: Jeff has just argued for intellectual integrity in the American adaptation. The room seems moved.
jokes.punchline: Pierce immediately follows Jeff's sincere, articulate appeal with a suggestion to replace the main character's companion with a sexualized blonde — undercutting everything Jeff said and characterizing exactly the kind of network thinking the speech argued against.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural placement — immediately after Jeff's sincere speech, Pierce suggests a blonde with a tennis racket. The contrast does the work. The specificity of 'tennis racket' is a nice absurdist detail that makes it funnier than a generic sexism joke.

jokes.text: Normally we don't concern ourselves with adultery, because then hotels wouldn't exist.
jokes.setup: Hotel staff have brought Nigel down because of a situation involving his wife.
jokes.punchline: The hotel manager's casual acknowledgment that adultery is basically their core business model — 'because then hotels wouldn't exist' — is a brilliantly cynical institutional aside.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The hotel manager's matter-of-fact cynicism about hotels and adultery is delivered with perfect deadpan authority. The logic is airtight and darkly funny — it's both a confession and a policy statement. High quotability, excellent economy. The character integration is lower because it's not Winger group-specific, but the joke stands alone very well.

jokes.text: Say your catchphrase. I'd rather not.
jokes.setup: Nigel (Thoraxis) has been brought to the hotel lobby in what is clearly an embarrassing personal situation involving his wife.
jokes.punchline: In the middle of the domestic crisis, a fan asks him to say his catchphrase. His flat 'I'd rather not' — given the circumstances — is the perfect deflation.
jokes.explanation: A callback that lands well in context. Asking someone to perform their villain catchphrase while their marriage is being confronted is perfectly awkward, and 'I'd rather not' is exactly the right response. Good economy and good cringe deployment.

jokes.text: What the hell is going on here? Suddenly our marriage isn't worth repairing? What? Wait, Nigel is married? That is so Thoraxis.
jokes.setup: Nigel's wife has confronted him in the hotel lobby. The situation is chaotic.
jokes.punchline: Annie's response to learning Nigel is married — 'That is so Thoraxis' — applies the fictional villain's characteristics to the real actor's real life infidelity. It's funny because she's using sci-fi character logic to process real human betrayal.
jokes.explanation: A sharp punchline — Annie using the fictional villain framework to judge real behavior is both funny and character-specific. 'That is so Thoraxis' is a quotable line that plays on the whole convention-world subplot.

jokes.text: And your American accent isn't at all convincing.
jokes.setup: Nigel has been practicing his American accent (joke #44). Now, in a moment of emotional confrontation, his wife calls it out.
jokes.punchline: The completely wrong-headed detail that Nigel's wife mentions — his accent, not the infidelity — reveals something funny about their relationship dynamic, and also pays off the earlier audition setup.
jokes.explanation: A callback that pays off the accent bit from earlier. In the middle of a confrontation about infidelity, criticizing the American accent is a funny misplaced priority and a good callback. Clean and economical.

jokes.text: I am sick of it, Jeff-- Nigel Winger.
jokes.setup: Nigel's wife is confronting him — but Annie has been playing 'Mrs. Winger' in the hotel, blurring the lines.
jokes.punchline: Nigel's wife calls him 'Jeff' before correcting to 'Nigel' — the correction from 'Jeff' to 'Nigel Winger' reveals the overlap between Annie's fantasy (Jeff Winger) and reality (Nigel's wife's real name being Winger, or the fantasy bleeding in). The stumble exposes the whole mess.
jokes.explanation: A clever structural joke — Nigel's wife says 'Jeff' (which is Annie's fantasy husband's name) before correcting herself. It tangles Annie's fiction with Nigel's reality in a satisfying way. The confusion is earned and the callback is well-constructed.

jokes.text: This day has turned crazy. I'm gonna go upstairs, towel off, and pray to God that I wake up in the middle of a final for a class I didn't know I was enrolled in.
jokes.setup: Jeff has witnessed the hotel lobby chaos — Nigel's wife confrontation, Annie's fantasy exposure, the convention nonsense.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's exit line deploys a classic anxiety dream — the 'final exam for a class you didn't attend' nightmare — as a preferable alternative to what he's just experienced. The specificity of the dream scenario is what makes it funny.
jokes.explanation: A good Jeff line — the universally relatable anxiety dream deployed as an escape fantasy is a clever inversion. The setup ('this day has turned crazy') followed by the specific escape scenario works well. The community college setting makes the exam dream doubly resonant.

jokes.text: Oh, honey. You went all psycho girlfriend on Abed, didn't you?
jokes.setup: Britta finds Troy looking dejected.
jokes.punchline: Britta calls Troy's behavior 'psycho girlfriend' — which both accurately describes what happened and is also a callback to Britta's own advice ('if you freak out, it's only gonna push Abed away'), plus the 'I'm not psycho!' line Troy said.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback — 'psycho girlfriend' mirrors Troy's own protest earlier. Britta's diagnosis is correct and her framing of it in romantic terms is consistent with the episode's running joke about Troy and Abed's relationship.

jokes.text: A quantum spanner. Yeah, it lights up or plays music or something.
jokes.setup: Britta gives Troy a quantum spanner (Inspector Spacetime prop) as a present to help reconcile with Abed.
jokes.punchline: Britta describes the item with complete vagueness — 'it lights up or plays music or something' — revealing she has zero understanding of what she bought or what it means to fans, but the gesture is sincere.
jokes.explanation: Very Britta — she did a thoughtful thing with zero actual knowledge of what she did. 'Lights up or plays music or something' is precisely the amount of research Britta would do. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Thank you. What?
jokes.setup: Abed has accepted Troy's reconciliation gesture and said 'thank you.' Troy seems surprised by the swift forgiveness.
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'What?' in response to Abed's 'thank you' — suggesting Troy expected more drama and is disarmed by the simplicity of the resolution — is a small, effective beat.
jokes.explanation: A quiet two-word beat that works. Troy's confusion at the easy resolution is a small character moment — he was braced for more conflict. Good economy.

jokes.text: Neurotypicals don't have the same focus you or I have. They always get distracted by marriage, kids, competitive cooking shows.
jokes.setup: Toby is making his pitch to Abed about their special connection as fans, suggesting their friends will eventually drift away.
jokes.punchline: Toby's list of distractions for 'neurotypicals' — marriage, kids, 'competitive cooking shows' — the mundane list being capped by 'competitive cooking shows' is the joke. It escalates from serious life events to a TV genre.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'marriage, kids' to 'competitive cooking shows' is the right absurdist pivot. It also functions as satire of the kind of fan who views normal life as distraction. The 'competitive cooking shows' specificity elevates it.

jokes.text: David doesn't exist. You're mad. Nothing you've said can prove that. You said his name was Andrew. Bollocks.
jokes.setup: Abed has caught Toby in a lie — 'Andrew' vs 'David' — and accuses him of inventing the friend.
jokes.punchline: Toby's defense ('Nothing you've said can prove that') followed immediately by being caught with a name contradiction, capped by 'Bollocks' — the rapid collapse of his lie in real time.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to a planted detail. The 'Nothing you've said can prove that' defense immediately failing is a good structure, and 'Bollocks' as Toby's capitulation word is characterful. Rewatch bonus for catching the name discrepancy earlier.

jokes.text: Maybe there's a reason the inspector always chooses a human companion. His human friends keep him grounded and invested in the world, like with me and Troy.
jokes.setup: Toby has been arguing that great people (inspectors) are inevitably abandoned by ordinary companions.
jokes.punchline: Abed reframes the Inspector Spacetime mythology to defend his human friendships — the meta-joke being that Community is doing exactly this: using a Doctor Who analogue to comment on Abed's own relationships. Abed is both in the metaphor and analyzing it.
jokes.explanation: A thematic joke as much as a structural one — Abed using his beloved show's mythology to argue for the value of ordinary human connection is exactly his character. The meta layer (Community using its show-within-a-show to comment on itself) gives it rewatch value.

jokes.text: If I could Winger you. Sure. I don't know what that means.
jokes.setup: Abed wants to make an argument and asks Jeff's permission to 'Winger' him.
jokes.punchline: Jeff agrees to 'Winger' before admitting he doesn't know what 'Winger' means as a verb — but his agreement is so reflexive that he consented before processing the ask. Also funny that Jeff's name has become a verb for his rhetorical speech style.
jokes.explanation: A smart joke about Jeff's established character trait (the inspiring speech) being so codified that it's become a verb within the group's vocabulary. Jeff's immediate assent followed by 'I don't know what that means' is the right beat. High character integration — this is very Community-specific.

jokes.text: Wait, wait. Toby, Toby. Toby, no. Wait just a second. Just playing a game.
jokes.setup: Troy has found where Toby locked Abed (or is about to do something physical). Troy intervenes.
jokes.punchline: The implied physical confrontation defused by 'Just playing a game' — Troy in full protective mode, trying to look casual while clearly not.
jokes.explanation: A transitional physical beat that is functional but not particularly well-crafted. The setup and payoff are thin. Mostly serves plot.

jokes.text: You have to let me out. Not until Stockholm syndrome sets in. How long do you think that will be, hours? Would you love me if I got you a churro?
jokes.setup: Jeff has apparently been locked in somewhere by Annie (or they're in a contained situation together).
jokes.punchline: Annie is hoping Stockholm syndrome will bond them, and her negotiation tool is a churro. The escalation from 'Stockholm syndrome' to 'churro' is a perfect deflation — she's planning captivity in a convention center.
jokes.explanation: A very funny bit. 'Not until Stockholm syndrome sets in' is an absurd framing of what Annie is doing, and the pivot to 'Would you love me if I got you a churro?' is a perfect escalation-through-deflation. The churro specifically is a great low-stakes absurdist choice. Good character integration — Annie's manipulative sweetness channeled through captivity.

jokes.text: I'm not sure how much air there is in here. And still you talk.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are confined together in a small space.
jokes.punchline: Jeff suggests the air supply is limited. Annie's response — 'And still you talk' — turns his complaint about oxygen scarcity into a critique of Jeff's own verbosity. The irony is perfect: he's the one talking.
jokes.explanation: A sharp, economical joke. The setup (not much air) and the punchline (Jeff is wasting it by talking) is a clean inversion where the complainer is the problem. 'And still you talk' is four words that do a lot of work. High quotability.

jokes.text: Troy will find me. / Who? / You know who Troy is. / Yeah. / Troy will find me.
jokes.setup: Abed reassures himself that Troy will rescue him. Toby plays dumb.
jokes.punchline: Abed says 'You know who Troy is' — Toby concedes 'Yeah' — and then Abed repeats 'Troy will find me' with renewed conviction. The whole exchange becomes a small ritual of mutual acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: Abed's quiet confidence in Troy is both touching and funny — especially coming immediately after the episodes-long thread about whether Troy still needs Abed. 'Troy will find me' repeated as a mantra shows Abed's faith in their friendship, and Toby's reluctant 'Yeah' admission is funny.

jokes.text: Troy will find me. Who? You know who Troy is. Yeah. Troy will find me.
jokes.setup: Abed is locked somewhere by Toby and asserts that Troy will come.
jokes.punchline: Toby pretends not to know who Troy is — the most deliberate and transparent attempt to diminish the Troy-Abed bond. Abed's patient repetition ('Troy will find me') is an expression of complete faith.
jokes.explanation: A good character moment — Abed's quiet, unshakeable faith in Troy is played against Toby's petty attempt to erase him. The repetition of 'Troy will find me' gains conviction with each iteration.

jokes.text: What is a gluon anyway? Can we stop talking about Abed?
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are confined together and talking.
jokes.punchline: Annie asks Jeff to stop talking about Abed — but Jeff was asking about a physics particle ('gluon'), not about Abed. The confusion reveals Annie is so preoccupied with Abed's situation (and their own conversation) that she's mishearing Jeff.
jokes.explanation: A quick mistaken-identity joke — Annie hears 'gluon' as a Abed-related discussion. The misunderstanding is slight but the economy is good and it generates a small laugh.

jokes.text: Britta and Jeff's gluon photo — Britta stops during the photo, can't go through with it, and tells Jeff to go to Abed.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are finally having their own moment, taking the gluon photo together.
jokes.punchline: Even their attempt to have a fun moment can't be completed because Britta can't stop thinking about Abed's situation — their 'couple time' is interrupted by platonic responsibility.
jokes.explanation: More of a plot beat than a joke, but it has comic irony — the gluon bonding photo, which represents friendship and eternal connection, is abandoned because of actual friendship loyalty.

jokes.text: For the first time in my long history of being locked inside things, I knew someone would come.
jokes.setup: Troy has rescued Abed from wherever Toby locked him.
jokes.punchline: Abed's matter-of-fact reference to having 'a long history of being locked inside things' — delivered as if this is a normal biographical detail — is both funny and deeply Abed.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Abed lines in the episode. 'My long history of being locked inside things' is a deadpan autobiographical detail that implies a rich, unstated history of exactly this kind of situation. The character integration is as high as it gets — only Abed would say this, and only Abed would have this history. The warmth of the moment (he trusted Troy) makes it land emotionally as well as comedically.

jokes.text: Saw the two robes, the two coffee cups, one with lipstick, one without. And I saw actual hair that looked a lot like mine on my side of the sink, so I have some questions.
jokes.setup: Jeff went to 'his' hotel room and found evidence of Annie's Mrs. Winger fantasy.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's forensic inventory of the room evidence — robes, cups, hair — is building to discovering Annie's fantasy, but his detective-style delivery escalates the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's methodical enumeration of evidence is a good setup for the reveal. The 'one with lipstick, one without' detail is a sharp specific. Functional setup for the following jokes.

jokes.text: First one, is that actually my hair? And, if so, did it fall out naturally? If it did, you need to tell me right now because I have to call science.
jokes.setup: Jeff found what appears to be his hair in the hotel room he wasn't using.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's first question about Annie's fantasy isn't about the relationship implications — it's about whether his hair is falling out. His vanity so completely overwhelms the interpersonal situation that he's ready to 'call science' about hair loss. The escalation to 'call science' is perfect.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Jeff finding his hair in an unoccupied room and his immediate, panicked response being entirely about hair loss — not the relationship implications — is perfect character comedy. 'I have to call science' as the escalation point is quotable and characterologically exact. Only Jeff Winger would respond to discovering someone's secret fantasy about him by worrying about baldness first. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: All right, I may have been play-acting that we were married and then the staff thought you were cheating, and I had to save face.
jokes.setup: Jeff is demanding an explanation for the Mrs. Winger situation.
jokes.punchline: Annie's explanation is so compressed and so bizarre — she was play-acting, then had to maintain the lie for hotel staff, the events spiraling — delivered with the casual tone of someone explaining why they were five minutes late.
jokes.explanation: Annie's explanation is a good character beat — the casual delivery of what is objectively a very strange situation. The 'I had to save face' as if this was the logical course of action is funny.

jokes.text: Do I have to worry about this? / No, I was just daydreaming. I've married you at least a half a dozen times. And Troy. And Zac Efron. Mostly Zac Efron.
jokes.setup: Jeff asks if he should worry about Annie's behavior. Annie reassures him it's just daydreaming.
jokes.punchline: Annie's disclosure escalates: she's married Jeff a half-dozen times in daydreams — and Troy, and Zac Efron — 'mostly Zac Efron.' The honesty and the rankings are both funny.
jokes.explanation: The progression Jeff → Troy → Zac Efron → 'mostly Zac Efron' is excellent. The fact that she's honest about all of it, the fact that Troy made the list, and especially 'mostly Zac Efron' as the clarifying detail that places Jeff firmly in third — it's a great joke with high quotability. Very Annie: candid oversharing that lands as both funny and slightly devastating for Jeff's ego.

jokes.text: Do I have to worry about this? No, I was just daydreaming. I've married you at least a half a dozen times. And Troy. And Zac Efron. Mostly Zac Efron.
jokes.setup: Jeff asks if he should be worried about Annie's behavior. Annie reassures him it's just daydreaming.
jokes.punchline: Annie reveals she's married Jeff 'at least a half a dozen times' in her head — but then adds Troy and Zac Efron, and the pivot to 'Mostly Zac Efron' completely reframes the previous admission. Jeff is suddenly far less special.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The escalation is perfect — 'I've married you at least a half a dozen times' is already a confession, then Troy is added (deflation), then Zac Efron, and then 'Mostly Zac Efron' as the kicker completely repositions Jeff from the object of the fantasy to a runner-up. The structure is tight, the character integration is high (this is very Annie), and the quotability is excellent. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Does Zac get a drink thrown in his face?
jokes.setup: Annie has just revealed that most of her fantasy marriages are with Zac Efron, not Jeff.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's question about whether Zac Efron also has drinks thrown in his face — presumably a reference to something that happened in this episode or the fantasy confrontation with Nigel's wife — reveals Jeff is now competing with Zac Efron for status in Annie's daydreams.
jokes.explanation: A good callback beat. Jeff's wounded ego manifesting as competitive comparison with Zac Efron is funny — he's essentially asking if he occupies the same narrative role in Annie's other fantasies. The character integration is good: Jeff can't resist the comparison.

jokes.text: I can tell you one thing your fantasy got wrong. If we were married, you wouldn't find me flirting with another woman in a hotel bar.
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining the flaws in Annie's fantasy of their marriage.
jokes.punchline: Jeff claims his fantasy self wouldn't flirt with another woman — which is both a sweet moment and immediately recognizable as probably false given everything we know about Jeff. The sincerity of the line is what makes it land, since the audience knows better.
jokes.explanation: A moment of Jeff semi-sincerely defending a fantasy version of himself with a claim the audience may or may not believe. The irony is light but present. Functions well as a bridge to the warm resolution.

jokes.text: Older? Not lame.
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining why some things Annie thinks are fun he wouldn't want to do — he stops himself before saying 'older.'
jokes.punchline: Annie immediately supplies 'Older?' and Jeff corrects to 'Not lame' — the gap between what he almost said (acknowledging their age difference) and what he recovers to (denying lameness) is the joke. He can't bring himself to admit the age issue.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-constructed two-beat exchange. Annie's immediate 'Older?' shows she's already thought about this. Jeff's 'Not lame' is the right deflection — he can't complete the sentence that would acknowledge their age difference honestly. Very economical.

jokes.text: An appletini. Oh, God, don't make me order that. Please?
jokes.setup: Jeff offers to buy Annie a drink as an olive branch.
jokes.punchline: Annie orders an appletini — the most stereotypically juvenile, unserious cocktail — and Jeff's pained response ('Oh, God, don't make me order that') reveals his status anxiety about being seen ordering it. Annie doubles down with 'Please?'
jokes.explanation: A good character beat — Annie's drink choice is perfect (youthful, sweet, embarrassing to order) and Jeff's distress at having to say 'appletini' aloud is very Jeff. The 'Please?' is the right ending. Leans slightly on established cocktail snobbery tropes but is well-deployed.

jokes.text: Heh. Appletini. That is so great.
jokes.setup: Jeff has ordered the appletini, apparently to the bartender.
jokes.punchline: Jeff laughing at himself for ordering an appletini — 'That is so great' in a tone that means the opposite — is a moment of rare self-deprecation from someone usually very protective of his image.
jokes.explanation: A callback payoff to the appletini setup. Jeff's self-deprecating amusement is a small character growth moment played for laughs. Functional and character-consistent.

jokes.text: And I have a surprise for you guys. Pow. Really pushing me here.
jokes.setup: The group is reunited at the hotel bar.
jokes.punchline: Abed produces something ('Pow') as a surprise. Jeff's 'Really pushing me here' — presumably in response to something Abed-ish — is a good straight-man beat.
jokes.explanation: A transitional beat without clear transcript context. Mildly amusing but difficult to score highly without knowing what 'Pow' refers to. Functional filler.

jokes.text: He's back. Do you mind if we crash this party? That we already crashed.
jokes.setup: Pierce and Shirley reappear at the hotel bar asking to 'crash the party.'
jokes.punchline: Abed's 'That we already crashed' — noting that Pierce and Shirley already crashed the original trip without being invited — is a small, precise callback.
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean callback that acknowledges the episode's through-line. Good economy and correct placement.

jokes.text: Pierce, Shirley, I'm glad you made it. It was rude of me not to invite you. Sorry. Just remember, Abed, I did my best. We both did.
jokes.setup: Abed genuinely apologizes to Pierce and Shirley for not inviting them.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's response — 'Just remember, I did my best. We both did.' — takes Abed's sincere apology and immediately frames it as his own moral victory, claiming credit for the reconciliation that just happened to him.
jokes.explanation: A good Pierce beat — his reflexive self-aggrandizement even when receiving an apology is very consistent character comedy. 'We both did' is the right note of collaborative self-congratulation.

jokes.text: Bow before Thoraxis! [Jeff performs the catchphrase, to everyone's phones/cameras.]
jokes.setup: Abed has apparently convinced Jeff to do the Thoraxis catchphrase for the group as a surprise.
jokes.punchline: Jeff — who earlier refused to be associated with the convention, wanted a bag over his head, and was horrified to be compared to a villain — is now performing the catchphrase for everyone's phones. The character arc is complete and the reversal is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff to Jeff's whole convention arc. His 180-degree reversal from 'I'd need a bag over my head' to 'Bow before Thoraxis!' is the comedic payoff of his through-line. Rewatch bonus for catching the full arc.

jokes.text: See, this is why I don't hang with you folks on the weekends.
jokes.setup: Jeff has just performed 'Bow before Thoraxis!' for the group.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate self-distancing from the moment he just created — 'See, this is why I don't hang with you folks on the weekends' — is a perfect Jeff move: participate fully, then immediately disavow.
jokes.explanation: A great Jeff beat — his reflexive cool-maintenance immediately after a moment of genuine fun is very character. The line is quotable and character-specific. The irony of using the moment he created as evidence for why he avoids these people is sharp.

jokes.text: Here we are, the 1960s, the greatest, grooviest period in the entire history of the entire universe.
jokes.setup: What appears to be an Inspector Spacetime-style coda or tag scene with Troy and Abed in character.
jokes.punchline: 'The greatest, grooviest period in the entire history of the entire universe' — the hyperbolic, 60s-speak claim about a specific decade is an affectionate parody of Doctor Who's sometimes overwrought narration.
jokes.explanation: A fun tag scene setting — Troy and Abed playing Inspector Spacetime is an established show tradition. The dialogue is affectionate parody. Not the sharpest writing but warm and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: The Inspector Spacetime in-universe show closing segment — Inspector and his companion discuss time and space travel, culminating in: 'I must sleep with the sexiest woman here who is also my grandmother. Or I will cease to exist.'
jokes.setup: An in-universe Inspector Spacetime scene plays — the Inspector explains he must sleep with someone.
jokes.punchline: The 'sexiest woman here' turns out to also be his grandmother — a time-travel paradox that necessitates incest for the Inspector's continued existence.
jokes.explanation: Good dark absurdist joke. The time-travel incest paradox is a staple of the genre (Back to the Future adjacent) but pushed to explicit absurdity. The Inspector's matter-of-fact framing makes it funnier than a dramatic version would be.

jokes.text: I'm lucky. I get to visit places like this because I can travel through time and space, but not both at once. Do you know why that is, ensign? Because, Inspector Spacetime, our minds would be blown with the space-time confusion.
jokes.setup: In the Inspector Spacetime tag, the inspector explains his travel limitations.
jokes.punchline: 'Our minds would be blown with the space-time confusion' — a deliberately clunky in-universe explanation that parodies how sci-fi shows paper over logical plot holes with pseudo-scientific gibberish. The earnestness of Troy's delivery of the terrible explanation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A parody of sci-fi exposition — the explanation is deliberately nonsensical in the way that actual sci-fi technobabble often is. 'Space-time confusion' as an official diagnosis is a good joke. Troy and Abed's commitment to playing it straight elevates it.

jokes.text: I get to visit places like this because I can travel through time and space, but not both at once.
jokes.setup: The Inspector is bragging about his abilities as a time traveler.
jokes.punchline: The limitation 'but not both at once' is a funny deflation — an omnipotent time traveler who can't multitask his fundamental abilities.
jokes.explanation: A good absurdist limitation on the character's powers. The parody of Doctor Who's budget constraints (they could rarely do both time AND space in the same episode) is well-observed. Good economy.

jokes.text: That's right. And now I must sleep with the sexiest woman here who is also my grandmother. Or I will cease to exist. How do you know I'm not your grandmother? There's only one way to find out.
jokes.setup: In the Inspector Spacetime tag, Abed's character delivers a time-travel plot point about needing to find his grandmother.
jokes.punchline: The Inspector must sleep with his grandmother (a classic bootstrap paradox/grandfather paradox joke from time travel fiction), and the companion's response — 'How do you know I'm not your grandmother?' followed by 'There's only one way to find out' — turns the sci-fi cliché into a darkly comedic sexual overture.
jokes.explanation: A good dark absurdist joke that plays on the time-travel grandfather paradox taken to its uncomfortable conclusion. 'There's only one way to find out' is the right sleazy punchline. The commitment to playing it straight in an Inspector Spacetime context makes it land. Rewatch bonus for catching the paradox logic.

jokes.text: I hate you.
jokes.setup: Troy (in character as the constable) has just been propositioned by Abed's inspector using the grandmother paradox.
jokes.punchline: 'I hate you' — the perfect, economical reaction that breaks character slightly while also being in-character. It's both Troy's real response to Abed's trolling and the constable's response to the inspector's gambit.
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfect economy, earns maximum economy score. As a closing line to the episode's tag, 'I hate you' captures the entire Troy-Abed dynamic in miniature: Abed does something absurd, Troy protests, but they both love it. The dual register (in-character/out-of-character) makes it a satisfying closer.

tmdb_overview: Troy worries about losing Abed to a fellow Inspector Spacetime fan at a convention for the show, while Annie fantasizes about being married to Jeff.
insight: Meta-heavy episode mines cringe from convention cosplay, lands 49 jokes in 41 minutes.
